subject: Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours

messages.author: 1c612257cd840ea8
messages.subject: Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours
parts:
Dear Vincent!

Within our validation study, we are now analyzing our Geneactiv data (measured over 7 days and 24 hours with 100 Hz). We set up the devices to start measuring on Monday 00:00, and the devices stopped (due to memory capacity) on Sunday 00:00.
Therefore, there was no mailing route or similar and participants brought back the devices on Tuesday or Wednesday. Since we do not have these "final 24 hours", we wonder if the non-wear time detection algorithm (used in the code and described below), may be a problem for us (e.g., erroneously classification of any active time as non-wear time due to the assumption of "device probably on mailing route")? Since the participants wore the devices on the last 24 hours, we do not want to erroneously classify any wear periods as non-wear periods...

“the final 24 hours are often considered the period in which the accelerometer is potentially taken off but moved because of transportation, e.g. by the mail service. All wear-periods in the final 24 hrs of each measurement shorter than three hours and preceded by at least one hour of non-wear time were classified as non-wear. Finally, if the measurement starts or ends with a period of less than three hours of wear followed by non-wear (any length) then this period of wear is classified as non-wear”



Would be great if you can give us some advice!!

Thank you very much for your help and maintaining the GGIR code!!



Best wishes from Graz, Austria!

Matteo Sattler

messages.author: 8d92e34685fbc6bd
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours
parts:
Dear Matteo,
It would be good to know what happens when you process the data? Do you get approximately 7 days of valid data for most of the recordings or do you see a lot of final days being lost as a result of the non-wear detection?
If so, then that would be an indication that we may need to facilitate an option to turn this aspect off for studies like yours.
I have not encountered this as a problem before, but let's see what your data tells us. 
Best wishes,
Vincent

messages.author: 1c612257cd840ea8
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours
parts:
Dear Vincent!

Thank you! We are going to check that but I think it should be fine. I will let you know soon.

However, in the meantime we wondered about our results. We tried different epoch lengths, filters and so on, just to compare the results. Interestingly, when we compare HFEN/BFEN with ENMO/LFENMO (lb = 0.2 Hz, hb = 20 Hz, n = 4; all other criteria were the same), HFEN/BFEN strongly overestimate time spent in MVPA by factors 3-7. This was the same for all MVPA variables in part2 and the same using hb = 15 Hz. Do you have any explanations for that? Could there be a problem in estimating these scores using a higher boundary in our sample/with our measurement frequency? Still, the correlations between the metrics are quite high r > 0.8 but the systematic difference is huge...

Thank you!

Best wishes,
Matteo

messages.author: 05de4f382b390d3d
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours
parts:
Dear Matteo,

As far as I know, the magnitude of the metrics provided by GGIR is not expected to be the same because of the influence of different filters to obtain them. Cut-points to classify MVPA have been proposed for ENMO, but not for the rest of the metrics, so I wouldn't expect MVPA estimates to be similar if you use different metrics and the same threshold (i.e., 100 mg by default in GGIR).

Hope this helps.

Best,
Jairo

parts:
Dear Jairo!

Thanks for the answer! So that may also be the reason why the average mg`s (even without application of any cut points) are substantially higher when using these high pass filtered metrics. Although these seems to be a bit strange? We have now compared the mean metrics in mg's (without those cut points) and the metrics are substantially higher (factor 3-4) for both HFEN and BFEN vs. ENMO/LFENMO.

Best,
Matteo

messages.author: 05de4f382b390d3d
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Non-wear time detection of the final 24 hours
parts:
Dear Matteo,

Yes, this is the reason, different filters produce different aggregation metrics. You can have a look on how they relate to each other and to energy expenditure in the 2013 paper by van Hees et al. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23626718). The magnitude is not expected to be the same. If they describe movement in a same way is something to be answered yet (as far as I know).

Best,
Jairo
